summary: Describes how language tags and ranges are used in LDAP, so directory values can be labeled with their natural language and clients can ask for values in languages they prefer.

eli5.summary: A phone book can list a name in several languages. This document says how to label each one and ask for the language you want.

questions: what is an ldap language tag
what is an ldap language range
how to search ldap by language
what does lang-en- mean in ldap
subtitle: How LDAP labels directory values with a natural language and lets clients search for the languages they want.

tldr.problem: Directory values such as names and addresses are human-readable text in some natural language, but LDAP had no clear rule for labeling that language or for asking the server for values in the languages a user prefers.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag option such as lang-en-US is added to an attribute description, and a language range option such as lang-en- matches every tag that begins with those subtags. Searches, compares, adds and modifies each treat the options in defined ways.
tldr.outcome: This is a Proposed Standard that replaces RFC 2596. It adds language ranges, a way for clients to discover server support, and clearer handling of attributes that carry several tags.

facts.label: Tag option form
facts.value: lang- followed by a language tag

facts.label: Range option form
facts.value: lang- with an optional tag and trailing hyphen

today: RFC 3866 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2004. It obsoletes RFC 2596, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Labeling Values with a Language
sections.content:
LDAP stores information as attributes of directory entries, and most attribute values are human-readable strings. RFC 3866 describes how language tags and language ranges, as defined in BCP 47 (RFC 3066), are carried in LDAP and how implementations interpret them. All LDAP implementations MUST be prepared to accept language tags and ranges.

A language tag is a string of ASCII letters and hyphens, such as fr, en-US or ja-JP, and tags are case insensitive. A language range is a set of tags: the range de matches the tags de and de-CH but not den, and a special wildcard range, a lone asterisk, matches all tags.

The RFC builds on LDAP attribute descriptions. An attribute description is the attribute type plus zero or more options. A description with options is a direct subtype of the same type with fewer options, so CN;x-bar;x-foo is a direct subtype of CN;x-bar and CN;x-foo, and CN is itself a subtype of name. This subtype rule drives all of the matching behavior below.
sections.eli5: Every piece of text in the directory can wear a little name tag saying which language it is in. Asking for a tag, or a whole family of tags, gets you just the labels you want.

sections.title: Language Tag Options
sections.content:
A language tag option is written as lang- followed by a BCP 47 language tag. The tag is a primary subtag of 1 to 8 letters, followed by any number of hyphen-separated subtags of 1 to 8 letters or digits. Examples of valid attribute descriptions are givenName;lang-en-US, CN;lang-ja, and SN;lang-de;lang-gem-PFL.

A description may carry several language tag options, and an entry may hold several attributes with the same type but different combinations of options. A language tag option has no effect on the syntax of the values or on how they are transferred.

Servers that store tagged attributes SHOULD allow any attribute type they recognize with the Directory String, IA5 String or another textual syntax to carry language tags, and MAY allow other types. Implementations MUST NOT look inside a tag when comparing two tags; they treat tags simply as strings of characters, and MUST accept any arbitrary string that fits the BCP 47 syntax. Clients SHOULD NOT assume a server can store tagged attributes at all.
sections.eli5: A tag looks like lang-en-US. The computer does not try to understand it; it just checks whether two labels are spelled the same.

sections.title: Search, Compare, Add and Modify
sections.content:
In a search filter, language tag options in an assertion must all be present on an attribute for it to match. The attribute type may be the same or a subtype. So a filter on name;lang-en-US with value Billy Ray matches CN;lang-en-US;x-foobar: Billy Ray and SN;lang-en-GB;lang-en-US: Billy Ray, but not CN;lang-en;x-foobar (different tag) or a plain name (no tag). The RFC warns that a tag in a filter hides values whose tag differs, so name;lang-en does NOT match name;lang-en-US. With no options in the assertion, only the type and value need to match.

In the requested attribute list, a request for name;lang-en returns name;lang-en and CN;lang-en;lang-ja but not SN or name;lang-fr. A client can list several descriptions, such as name;lang-en and name;lang-fr, to allow either. If the client asks for all attributes, or for an attribute with no language option, values are returned regardless of their tags.

A compare is treated like an equality filter. If no attribute has the same type (or a subtype) and each presented option, the server returns noSuchAttributeType. For example, comparing name with Johann against an entry holding givenName;lang-de-DE: Johann gives compareTrue, while comparing name;lang-de fails with noSuchAttributeType.

On add, a client may supply the same attribute type and value several times as long as each copy has a different set of language options. On modify, types and options MUST match exactly against stored values: to delete a tagged value you must name its tags, and to delete an untagged value you must give none.

If a server cannot store language tag options, it treats a tagged description as an unrecognized attribute. A search assertion with a tag then simply does not match (a presence assertion evaluates to FALSE and other assertions to Undefined, with no error), tagged attributes in a requested list are ignored, compare returns noSuchAttributeType, and add or modify fails with an appropriate result code if the server forbids unrecognized attributes.
sections.eli5: If you ask for English, you only get things with an English label, and the label has to be there. If you do not ask for any language, you get everything, in every language.

sections.title: Language Ranges
sections.content:
Since RFC 2596, it became clear that clients need to request values by a set of tags that all begin with the same subtags. A language range option is written lang- optionally followed by a language tag and a trailing hyphen, as in givenName;lang-en-, CN;lang- or SN;lang-de-;lang-gem-.

A range option matches a tag option if the range without its trailing hyphen equals the tag exactly, or if the range (with its hyphen) matches a prefix of the tag. The range option lang- matches every language tag option. Ranges are used in assertions, requested attribute lists and similar places, but they are not tagging options: attributes cannot be stored with a range option, and an attempt to add or update one is treated as an undefined attribute type and results in an error. Servers SHOULD support range assertions for any attribute type they allow to be stored with tags.

The matching rules mirror those for tags. A filter on name;lang-en- with value Billy Ray matches name;lang-en-US, CN;lang-en;x-foobar and SN;lang-en-GB;lang-en-US, but not untagged values. A request for name;lang-en- returns name;lang-en-US and CN;lang-en;lang-ja but not SN or name;lang-fr. A compare of name;lang- with Johann succeeds against a givenName;lang-de-DE value, because lang- matches any tag.
sections.eli5: A range is like asking for every shelf whose label starts with the same word. Ask for lang-en- and you get plain English and every kind of English, such as US or GB.

sections.title: Discovering Support
sections.content:
A server SHOULD advertise that it can store attributes with language tag options by publishing the object identifier 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.4 as a value of the root DSE. It SHOULD advertise language range matching by publishing 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.5 as a value of the supportedFeatures attribute in the root DSE, as defined in RFC 3674.

A server MAY limit language tag options to a subset of the attribute types it recognizes. The RFC does not define any way to find out which subset, so clients cannot discover that restriction through this specification.
sections.eli5: A server can put up a sign saying that it understands language labels. Clients look for the sign before using them.

sections.title: Working with Non-supporting Software
sections.content:
Implementers should make sure that tagged values do not break software that does not know about language tags. By the LDAP rule from RFC 2251, an attribute description with options is treated as a subtype of the type without options. A non-supporting server treats a description with language options as an unrecognized attribute type. A non-supporting client either does the same or treats it as any other unknown subtype, and typically ignores unrecognized subtypes of attributes it requests.

Two rules follow. Supporting clients SHOULD populate entries with untagged values as well as tagged ones, so non-supporting clients still see something. And supporting clients SHOULD be prepared to meet entries that have no tagged values at all.
sections.eli5: Some people do not read the labels. So you also keep an unlabeled copy for them, and you do not panic when you find an entry with no labels.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
Language tag and range options only indicate the native language of values and let clients ask for values that suit them. They are not known to raise specific security considerations, though the reader should consider the general directory security issues in RFC 3377.

The IANA registration of the two protocol mechanisms is described as completed: object identifier 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.4 is Language Tag Options and 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.5 is Language Range Options, both with usage Feature. The OpenLDAP Foundation assigned them under its private enterprise allocation.
sections.eli5: A language label is just a label, so it does not add new dangers. The two ID numbers for the features are written down in an official list.

data.title: Language tag option syntax
data.code:
language-tag-option = "lang-" Language-Tag

Language-Tag = Primary-subtag *( "-" Subtag )
Primary-subtag = 1*8ALPHA
Subtag = 1*8(ALPHA / DIGIT)
